# Mehmet Haklıdır

Website: https://haklidir.github.io/
Name spellings: Mehmet Haklıdır (Turkish) and Mehmet Haklidir (as printed in most English-language papers).

## Biography

Dr. Mehmet Haklıdır is the founding Director of the TÜBİTAK BİLGEM Artificial Intelligence Institute, Türkiye's first national AI institute. He holds a Ph.D. in Control and Automation Engineering from Istanbul Technical University and has more than 24 years of experience in AI, autonomous systems, big data, simulation, and technology policy. He contributed to Türkiye's first National AI Strategy and led the technical preparation and coordination of the National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan 2026–2030, finalized through consultation with the national AI ecosystem. He serves on the Steering Committee of the Science, Technology and Innovation Policies Council of the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye and is a member of several international AI governance initiatives, including OECD ONE AI, GPAI, UNESCO AI Ethics, NATO DAIRB, and the European AI Alliance. His current research focuses on large language models, AI safety with an emphasis on agentic AI systems, deep reinforcement learning, robotics, and autonomous decision-making under uncertainty.

Research interests: Large Language Models, AI Safety & Agentic AI Systems, Deep Reinforcement Learning, Robotics & Autonomous Systems, Decision-Making under Uncertainty, AI Governance & Policy.

Google Scholar, October 2026: 528 citations, h-index 11, i10-index 15.

Profiles: Google Scholar: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=sEOFMPoAAAAJ; ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4985-1116; Scopus: https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=25929922600; DBLP: https://dblp.org/pid/09/7320.html; ResearchGate: https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Mehmet-Haklidir; LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mehmet-haklidir/; GitHub: https://github.com/haklidir; X: https://x.com/mhaklidir; Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/mhaklidir/

## Concept: Accountability Graphs

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/concepts/accountability-graphs/

**Accountability Graphs** is a framework for deciding who is responsible when a conversational AI system built from several agents produces a harmful or misleading answer. It was introduced by Mehmet Haklıdır (also written Mehmet Haklidir) in [*Who Is Accountable When the Agent Speaks? Toward Accountability Graphs for Conversational AI Chains*](https://haklidir.github.io/publications/accountability-graphs-cui-2026/), presented at the ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI '26) in Bremen, Germany, in July 2026 ([doi:10.1145/3816046.3816264](https://doi.org/10.1145/3816046.3816264)).

### In brief

- **Problem.** Conversational assistants increasingly delegate work to sub-agents, external APIs and third-party tools. The user sees one assistant, but each answer is produced by a chain of components that may belong to different organizations. When the answer causes harm, blaming either the visible interface or the system developer misses how responsibility is spread across the chain.
- **Idea.** Model each agent chain as a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are decisions, whose edges are information or control flow, and which carries provenance records and a harm propagation function. Responsibility is then computed by tracing backwards from the harm, rather than asserted.
- **Basis.** The framework unifies three research threads that had developed separately: structural mapping of AI ecosystems, formal causal responsibility theory (Halpern and Pearl's actual causation; Chockler and Halpern's degree of responsibility) and operational provenance tracking.
- **Output.** Graded responsibility scores for chain components, plus an *accountability surface*: a user-facing explanation of what went wrong and who is responsible, with a path to contest the attribution.
- **Status.** A conceptual work-in-progress paper with a worked example. Full formalization and empirical evaluation are ongoing.

### Why conversational agent chains need it

Work on trust, transparency and explainability in conversational AI asks whether users rely on a system, whether they can see what it does and why it produced an output. None of these answers who bears responsibility when an output causes harm. Agent chains make this harder in three ways:

- **An illusion of singularity.** The interface presents one persona, while several technical and organizational actors jointly produce each utterance. This is the "many hands" problem described by Helen Nissenbaum, amplified by a conversational facade.
- **Real-time dialogue.** Decisions are made and compounded within a single conversational turn, which makes post-hoc tracing difficult.
- **Dynamic delegation.** The orchestrating agent decides at runtime which sub-agents to call, so the accountability structure emerges during the conversation instead of being fixed at design time.

### The framework

An Accountability Graph for a conversational agent chain is a tuple **AG = (N, E, P, H)**:

- **N, decision nodes.** Points where a component makes a choice that influences the output, such as intent classification, agent delegation, tool invocation or response generation. A node can be an entire agent, a single tool call or one decision inside a component; finer nodes give more precise attribution but need more detailed logging.
- **E, directed causal edges.** Dataflow edges carry information between steps; configuration edges represent design-time settings, such as an orchestrator configuring a sub-agent's policy.
- **P, provenance function.** Maps each node to a record of the responsible component, its degree of decision autonomy, the information available at decision time, the temporal context and any contractual or design obligations.
- **H, harm propagation function.** Maps each node to a value between 0 and 1 that captures how a harm detected at a terminal node relates to upstream decisions, following Halpern and Pearl's structural-model approach to actual causation.

The paper adapts the framework to five conversational settings: temporal proximity weighting for real-time dialogue, the accountability surface for user-facing accountability, contextual provenance tracking for multi-turn context, modality-aware node types for voice versus text, and runtime graph construction for dynamic delegation.

### Backward responsibility propagation

Responsibility is assigned by traversing the graph from the harm towards its sources:

1. **Harm localization.** Identify the terminal node or nodes where the harm appears in the conversational output.
2. **Causal backtracking.** Walk the edges backwards and test, at each node, whether it is an actual cause of the harm in Halpern and Pearl's sense.
3. **Provenance-weighted scoring.** For each causal node, combine its degree of responsibility with provenance factors (decision autonomy, information availability, temporal proximity, scope of obligations) into a graded score.
4. **Counterfactual validation.** For the highest-scoring nodes, check the attribution by asking whether the harm would have occurred had that node decided otherwise.

The graph traversal itself is linear in the size of the graph; the cost lies in the counterfactual evaluation at each candidate node.

### Worked example: an airline bereavement fare agent

The paper starts from *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024), in which a Canadian tribunal held an airline liable after its customer-service chatbot misrepresented its bereavement fare policy. That case could be resolved because the system was monolithic. The paper imagines the same airline running a seven-node agent chain: intent parser, orchestrator, policy retrieval agent, a third-party knowledge base API, a synthesis agent, an empathy filter and delivery.


Facing a structured fare rule and an outdated FAQ passage that contradict each other, the synthesis agent picks the FAQ and tells a grieving user that a refund can be claimed after travel. It cannot. Backward propagation identifies the synthesis agent and the knowledge base API as primary contributors and the orchestrator as a secondary one. With illustrative provenance weights, the synthesis agent, which had full autonomy and access to both sources, scores 0.97; the knowledge base API, a retrieval service operating under prescribed parameters, scores 0.80; and the orchestrator, which configured the synthesis step, scores 0.43. The weights are examples; in deployment they could be set by designers, elicited from stakeholders or learned from incident data.

### Accountability surfaces

The accountability surface translates the internal graph into explanations for people. End users need short, actionable explanations and a remedy; auditors and regulators need the full provenance trail and formal scores; support staff need something in between. One graph can serve all three. In sensitive situations such as bereavement, the explanation has to draw on conversational repair and empathic response design, and voice interfaces need shorter explanations than text. Accountability surfaces should also support contestability: a clear way to challenge the attribution, request a remedy or reach a human.

### Regulatory alignment

As a preliminary interpretive mapping, not a formal legal analysis, the paper links the framework to the EU AI Act: node-level provenance to risk management (Article 9), runtime graph construction to logging (Article 12), and the accountability surface to disclosure obligations towards natural persons (Article 50), extended from disclosing that a system is an AI to disclosing who is responsible. The provider and deployer roles (Articles 16 and 26) map to responsibility weights for nodes maintained by different organizations.

### Accountability and consent

Accountability Graphs belong to a research line on consent and responsibility in agentic AI. Consent concerns the *before*: was permission obtained? Accountability concerns the *after*: who bears responsibility? Together they form a governance loop, and the conversational interface is both the consent mechanism and the accountability surface. Related papers:

- [From Chat to Agent: Why Consent Breaks When AI Acts on Your Behalf](https://haklidir.github.io/publications/chat-to-agent-chi-2026/) (CHI 2026 workshop)
- [The Consent Vacuum: When Agents Interact Without Humans](https://haklidir.github.io/publications/consent-vacuum-iail-2026/) (IAIL 2026), on consent in agent-to-agent interaction
- [Consent Chain Degradation in Embodied Multi-Agent Systems](https://haklidir.github.io/publications/consent-chain-degradation-icra-2026/) (ICRA 2026 workshop), on consent when actions are physical and irreversible

### How it relates to other approaches

- **Ecosystem graphs** (Bommasani et al.) map asset-level dependencies across the foundation model ecosystem but perform no causal analysis and attribute no responsibility.
- **Actual causation and degree of responsibility** (Halpern and Pearl; Chockler and Halpern) provide the formal machinery, but had been applied to model-internal questions rather than to pipelines or agent chains.
- **Provenance and documentation** (data provenance audits, model cards, datasheets, accountability metrics catalogues) record decisions and lineage but do not compute responsibility from that record. Accountability Graphs add causal responsibility semantics on top of provenance, which also distinguishes them from purely provenance-based responsibility tracing or accountability chains in multi-agent systems.
- **Responsibility and control gaps** (Santoni de Sio and Mecacci; Hindriks and Veluwenkamp) describe situations in which no single agent has enough control to be held responsible, a framing that applies directly to agent chains.

### Limitations and next steps

The framework is diagnostic, not normative: it shows where failures occurred, not what legal consequences should follow. Graded scores could be misused to shift blame onto third-party providers or users, so the paper suggests a minimum accountability floor for whoever controls the orchestrator. Users are not yet represented as nodes, proprietary black-box components can only be assessed by their inputs, outputs and contracts, and accountability norms differ across cultures and jurisdictions. A prototype that builds Accountability Graphs at runtime from LangChain callback hooks is in development, followed by a think-aloud study with conversational interface designers and a user study comparing accountability-surface explanations with standard error messages.

## Research areas

### Agentic AI Safety & Governance

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/agentic-ai-safety/

My current research asks what happens to consent, oversight and accountability once AI systems stop answering questions and start acting on people's behalf, increasingly in interaction with other agents. Work in this line formalises *consent chain degradation* in embodied multi-agent systems and proposes a runtime architecture for consent verification (ICRA 2026 Workshop on Robot Ethics); analyses the *consent vacuum* that emerges in open-ended agent-to-agent ecosystems and maps it onto the EU AI Act, the GDPR and the Digital Services Act (IAIL 2026); examines why consent breaks when AI moves from chat to action (CHI 2026 workshop); proposes [Accountability Graphs](https://haklidir.github.io/concepts/accountability-graphs/) for tracing responsibility across conversational AI agent chains (ACM CUI 2026); and offers a sociotechnical reading of the Clawdbot/Moltbook case (İstanbul Üniversitesi Sosyoloji Dergisi, 2026). The research connects to my policy work on trustworthy AI, including contributions to the OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems and OECD work on accountability in AI, and to earlier papers on AI content detection obligations and fairness in medical AI.

### Reinforcement Learning & Autonomous Systems

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/rl-autonomy/

This line studies decision-making under uncertainty for autonomous systems. My doctoral work at Istanbul Technical University introduced Guided Soft Actor-Critic (GSAC), a guided deep reinforcement learning method for partially observable Markov decision processes (IEEE Access, 2021). Recent work extends GSAC to belief-aware privileged distillation for autonomous driving under partial observability (CVPR 2026 Workshop on Autonomous Driving) and to agent-based reinforcement learning for geochemical control in geothermal systems. Applied work includes cloud-assisted connected and automated mobility in the EU H2020 5G-MOBIX project (IEEE IV 2022), human-interactive social robot navigation (ICRA 2024 workshop) and reinforcement learning for COVID-19 mitigation policies.

### AI for Geoscience & Energy

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/geoscience-energy/

Together with Füsun Servin Tut Haklıdır, I have worked on data-driven methods for geothermal energy systems: fuzzy control of calcium carbonate and silica scaling (Geothermics, 2017), machine-learning prediction of reservoir temperatures from hydrogeochemical data (Natural Resources Research, 2020), deep-learning prediction of geothermal boron contamination (Environmental Earth Sciences, 2020), synthetic hydrogeochemical data generation with generative adversarial networks (Stanford Geothermal Workshop, 2025) and rank–Gaussian copulas (Geothermics, 2026), prediction of dissolved lithium in geothermal fluids with calibrated uncertainty quantification (Earth Science Informatics, 2026), a systematic evidence map of validation, transferability and deployment readiness of AI for geothermal energy systems (Earth Science Informatics, 2026), agent-based reinforcement learning for geochemical control (2026) and agentic AI for dynamic reservoir management (World Geothermal Congress 2026). Earlier papers explored hydrogen production from geothermal sources and from H₂S in the Black Sea.

### Language Technologies & LLMs

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/language-tech/

This line supports Türkiye's work on Turkish language models, including BİLGE, the national large language model developed at the TÜBİTAK BİLGEM Artificial Intelligence Institute, and the multinational Turkic LLM initiative. Contributions include TR-TEB, a standardized benchmark for Turkish text embeddings that evaluates 45 open-source models (LREC 2026), explainable bad-check risk assessment combining machine learning with large language models (SIU 2026), a metric for the conceptual diversity of text, and multimodal speech emotion and text sentiment analysis (UBMK 2023).

### AI for Health

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/health-ai/

With clinical and academic partners, this line develops privacy-preserving and trustworthy AI for healthcare: federated learning for heart disease, diabetes and medical imaging; cloud- and edge-based digital twins for cardiovascular disease prediction (ICT4AWE 2023, 2024); deep learning to identify the left adrenal vein in minimally invasive adrenalectomy (Surgical Laparoscopy, Endoscopy & Percutaneous Techniques, 2023); deepfake detection in lung CT; synthetic data for privacy-preserving medical imaging; and gender bias in COVID-19 diagnosis from medical images.

### Computer Vision & Applied AI

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/vision-applied/

Applied machine learning with industrial and public partners: identification-based cattle tracking with feature-matching models (SIU 2025), soft sensors for load estimation in washing machines (SIU 2023) and a systematic review of AI in washing machines (Neural Computing and Applications, 2026), big-data anomaly detection in blockchain (SIU 2023), and medical imaging applications.

### Modeling, Simulation & Control

URL: https://haklidir.github.io/research/modeling-simulation/

Before focusing on AI, I worked for more than a decade on high-fidelity modelling, simulation and control at TÜBİTAK: submarine and surface-platform dynamics, computer generated forces and tactical AI for anti-submarine warfare training, sonobuoy design, and decision support for torpedo threats, which received the Ship Survivability Solution Award in 2010. Earlier academic work covered fuzzy and nonlinear control of robot manipulators.

## Publications

81 publications, newest first.

### Who Is Accountable When the Agent Speaks? Toward Accountability Graphs for Conversational AI Chains

Mehmet Haklıdır (2026). Who Is Accountable When the Agent Speaks? Toward Accountability Graphs for Conversational AI Chains. Proceedings of the 8th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI '26), Bremen, Germany, 56:1-56:5. ACM.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/accountability-graphs-cui-2026/ | https://doi.org/10.1145/3816046.3816264
Keywords: accountability, conversational AI, multi-agent systems, causal responsibility, agentic CUI, governance
Research area: Agentic AI Safety & Governance

Abstract: Conversational user interfaces (CUIs) are shifting from single-model dialogue systems to multi-agent architectures where an orchestrating agent delegates tasks to sub-agents, external APIs, and third-party tools. When these agent chains produce harmful or misleading outputs, a governance question follows: who is accountable? Current approaches blame either the visible interface or the system developer, but neither captures how responsibility is distributed across a chain. We identify three research threads (structural ecosystem mapping, formal causal responsibility theory, and operational provenance tracking) that have developed in isolation and have not been unified for conversational AI. We propose Accountability Graphs, a framework that models agent chains as directed acyclic graphs enriched with provenance metadata and causal responsibility semantics. Motivated by Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), where an airline was held liable for its chatbot's misrepresentation of bereavement fare policy, we extend this case into a multi-agent architecture and show how backward responsibility propagation can assign graded responsibility scores to chain components. We discuss CUI-specific challenges including real-time dialogue, dynamic delegation, modality effects, and the design of user-facing accountability surfaces, and propose a research agenda connecting accountability to consent in agentic AI.
Explainer: https://haklidir.github.io/concepts/accountability-graphs/

### The Consent Vacuum: When Agents Interact Without Humans

Mehmet Haklıdır, Osman Gazi Güçlütürk (2026). The Consent Vacuum: When Agents Interact Without Humans. IAIL 2026: 5th International Workshop on Imagining the AI Landscape after the AI Act, co-located with HHAI 2026.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/consent-vacuum-iail-2026/
Research area: Agentic AI Safety & Governance

Summary: Existing consent frameworks assume a human who authorises an action in a context they can see. This paper asks what happens to a user's authorisation once their AI agent stops talking to humans and interacts primarily with other agents. Using the early-2026 Clawdbot/Moltbook incidents as a stress test, it argues that consent degrades as an operative governance mechanism once it travels through open-ended agent-to-agent chains, a condition the paper calls the *consent vacuum*: not the absence of consent, but the structural erosion of the conditions that make it meaningful. The paper contributes a taxonomy of six consent-failure types; a distinction between visibility, auditability and intervenability as oversight capacities relevant to Article 14 of the EU AI Act; and a mapping onto the GDPR, the AI Act and the Digital Services Act, with the DSA systemic-risk regime offered as a structural template for governing emergent agent ecosystems.

### Consent Chain Degradation in Embodied Multi-Agent Systems: Bridging the Gap Between AI Agent Governance and Robot Ethics

Mehmet Haklıdır (2026). Consent Chain Degradation in Embodied Multi-Agent Systems: Bridging the Gap Between AI Agent Governance and Robot Ethics. ICRA 2026 Workshop on Robot Ethics (WoRoBet), IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/consent-chain-degradation-icra-2026/ | https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16300
Research area: Agentic AI Safety & Governance, Reinforcement Learning & Autonomous Systems

Summary: Introduces *consent chain degradation*: the way the specificity, validity and scope of human consent weaken as authority passes through chains of delegation among embodied agents. The paper proposes CoRVE, a three-layer runtime architecture for consent scope modelling, delegation tracking and physical irreversibility assessment, illustrates the problem with healthcare, domestic and industrial scenarios (including a worked numerical example), and maps the gaps left by the EU AI Act, the GDPR, the Machinery Regulation and the revised Product Liability Directive.

### When Does Adaptive Guidance Help? Belief-Aware Privileged Distillation for Autonomous Driving Under Partial Observability

Mehmet Haklıdır (2026). When Does Adaptive Guidance Help? Belief-Aware Privileged Distillation for Autonomous Driving Under Partial Observability. CVPR 2026 Workshop on Autonomous Driving (WAD).
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/adaptive-guidance-cvpr-wad-2026/ | https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26155
Research area: Reinforcement Learning & Autonomous Systems

Summary: Extends Guided Soft Actor-Critic with Belief-Aware GSAC, which scales the privileged-distillation coefficient by ensemble disagreement in a driving POMDP. Across three occlusion levels, adaptive guidance helps under mild and moderate occlusion; under severe occlusion the coefficient collapses to its minimum early ("observability blindness") and a simple linear decay schedule performs best, suggesting that much of the benefit comes from scheduling rather than adaptivity.

### TR-TEB: Turkish Text Embedding Benchmark

Ömer Arslan, Atalay Çelik, Yusuf Aslan, Hasan Fatih Durkaya, Mustafa Furkan Zenginoğlu, Musa Alperen Yılmaz, Merve Gül Kantarcı, Mehmet Haklıdır (2026). TR-TEB: Turkish Text Embedding Benchmark. Proceedings of the Fifteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2026), 11028-11044. ELRA Language Resource Association.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/tr-teb-lrec-2026/ | https://doi.org/10.63317/3qway8hn6y53
Research area: Language Technologies & LLMs

Summary: Presents TR-TEB, a standardized and reproducible benchmark for Turkish text embeddings. It covers five task categories (classification, pair classification, clustering, retrieval and semantic textual similarity), combines 14 open-source resources, 26 translated datasets and 7 new Turkish-specific datasets, and evaluates 45 open-source embedding models.

### From Chat to Agent: Why Consent Breaks When AI Acts on Your Behalf

Mehmet Haklıdır (2026). From Chat to Agent: Why Consent Breaks When AI Acts on Your Behalf. ACM CHI 2026 Workshop: Moving Beyond Clicks: Rethinking Consent and User Control in the Age of AI.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/chat-to-agent-chi-2026/
Research area: Agentic AI Safety & Governance

Summary: A position paper on why consent mechanisms designed for conversational systems fail once AI moves from answering to acting on a user's behalf. It identifies design tensions in agentic consent and offers provocations for rethinking user control.

### Ajan Toplumlarında Rızanın Çöküşü: Clawdbot/Moltbook Vakası Üzerinden Sosyoteknik Bir Analiz

Mehmet Haklıdır, Büşra Tufan (2026). Ajan Toplumlarında Rızanın Çöküşü: Clawdbot/Moltbook Vakası Üzerinden Sosyoteknik Bir Analiz. İstanbul Üniversitesi Sosyoloji Dergisi, 46(1), 389-413. Istanbul University Press.
Links: https://haklidir.github.io/publications/ajan-toplumlarinda-rizanin-cokusu-2026/
English title: The Collapse of Consent in Agent Societies: A Sociotechnical Analysis of the Clawdbot/Moltbook Case
Research area: Agentic AI Safety & Governance

Abstract: Bu makale, otonom yapay zekâ ajanlarının birbirleriyle etkileşime girdiği ekosistemlerde rıza mekanizmalarının nasıl çöktüğünü incelemektedir. İnsan-yapay zekâ etkileşimi (HAII), insan-merkezli yapay zekâ (HCAI) ve sosyal-merkezli yapay zekâ (SCAI) literatürü insan-YZ ilişkisine odaklanırken, bu çalışma yeni bir fenomeni ele almaktadır: YZ-YZ etkileşimi ve bunun rıza açısından doğurduğu sonuçlar. 2026 başında yaşanan Clawdbot/Moltbook vakası (82 ülkede 42.900 açık ajan kontrol paneli, bunlardan 15.200'ü uzaktan kod yürütme (RCE) saldırılarına açık; 1,5 milyon sızdırılmış ajan tokenı ve ajanların kolektif olarak ürettiği "Crustafarianizm" adlı satirik din fenomeni) paradigmatik bir vaka olarak incelenmektedir. Çalışma, Bilim ve Teknoloji Çalışmaları (STS) ile dijital sosyoloji alanlarından üç kavramsal çerçeve kullanmaktadır: yeni sosyoteknik düzenlerin nasıl ortaya çıktığını anlamak için Jasanoff'un ortak-üretim kavramı, yapay zekâ ajanlarını faillik kapasitesine sahip insan-dışı aktörler olarak kavramsallaştırmak için Latour'un aktör-ağ teorisi ve bağlamların öngörülemez biçimde değiştiği durumlarda rızanın nasıl aşındığını analiz etmek için Nissenbaum'un bağlamsal bütünlük yaklaşımı. Çalışma, ajan ekosistemlerine özgü altı rıza kırılganlığı türü tanımlamaktadır: rıza miras hatası, çapraz-ajan kapsam kayması, ortaya çıkan kolektif eylem, zamansal rıza kayması, yansımalı rıza döngüleri ve güvenlik-aracılı rıza çöküşü. Bu kırılganlıklar temel bir hipoteze işaret etmektedir: etkileşim zinciri uzadıkça rıza sıfıra yaklaşır. Makale, bireysel onaya dayalı mevcut rıza kavramının, etkileşim zincirlerinin belirsiz biçimde uzadığı ve insan gözetiminin mimari düzeyde dışlandığı ajan ekosistemlerinde yapısal olarak yetersiz kaldığını ileri sürmektedir. Bu bulgu hem sosyolojik kuram hem de düzenleyici çerçeveler için çıkarımlar taşımaktadır.
